Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "
hey, can you turn this into a practical plan for the next two months for the little antique clock room we run in the old Mercer Street print shop. we have six volunteers, but only me, Jo, and Malik are usually there on Tuesdays. the room is open to visitors two Saturdays a month, and we're hoping to do a slightly bigger open afternoon at the end of the eight weeks, probably the 14th, though the landlord hasn't confirmed we can use the back room that day. please keep it realistic for a volunteer group, not a full museum staff, and show what needs deciding versus what we can do now.

there are 18 clocks in the room at the moment. five are wall clocks, four mantel clocks, three longcase clocks, and the rest are small travel or desk clocks. two of the longcases are not running; one has a cracked glass panel and a label that says “please don't wind.” don't tell us to test it. the other stops after about twenty minutes, but Malik hasn't looked inside yet. the wall clock with the blue painted face came from Jo's aunt and we have no paperwork for it. we do have a receipt for the small brass carriage clock, but the date on it is smudged. please include a sensible way to keep track of these differences without pretending we know dates, makers, or values.

we're trying to sort out what visitors can see, and how to keep the room safe while we do that. the narrow aisle by the tall case is about 70 centimetres across, and the side door opens into it; that's the exit visitors use. there's a low radiator under the front window and a box of old pendulums currently sits on the floor beside it. the ceiling lights flicker sometimes, especially when the kettle is on, and the only socket near the display bench is loose. we have a folding table, two lamps, three paper signs, and a small lockable cabinet, but no display stands. don't assume we can buy much. ask us to get the electrical issue checked, but don't tell us to repair wiring ourselves. I'd like the plan to say how the clocks, tools, and visitor route might be arranged before the open afternoon.

we also need a basic routine for the clocks, but we don't have a conservator and shouldn't take anything apart just to make it look busy. Jo can clean the outside cases with a dry cloth, and Malik is comfortable checking whether a clock is already running, but neither of them is trained to oil or adjust a movement. one volunteer, Priya, has offered to contact a local horologist; we don't know whether they can visit or what they charge. please include what we can safely record in the meantime, how to label anything that shouldn't be touched, and what questions to ask the horologist without assuming they'll agree to do the work.

our records are spread across a notebook, two phone photo folders, and a spreadsheet that was last updated in January. the notebook has a few handwritten entries like “runs well” with no date or initials. photos often show the clock but not its back, label, or condition. we can probably spend one Tuesday making a shared list, but not a whole day. I want a record that volunteers can update after a visit, with a clear difference between something observed and something we were told. include a simple way to note an uncertain detail and who entered it, and don't suggest throwing away the old notes or changing the spreadsheet before we've checked what's already there.

for the visitors, we want a short explanation of how a mechanical clock works, but nobody has agreed to give a talk. Jo might welcome people and Malik may be able to demonstrate winding a clock that is cleared for it, though he doesn't want that presented as a promise. one visitor last month asked, “Is the ticking meant to sound uneven?” We didn't know which clock they meant. please make the plan leave room for questions and avoid claiming every clock is working or original. we have a magnifying glass, a few old trade catalogues, and a printed map showing where some of the clocks were collected; the map has two pencil marks we can't identify.

we need to check permissions too. the shop is rented, the landlord allows the regular Saturday opening, and we haven't asked about extra chairs, a banner on the pavement, or use of the back room. the fire instructions are in a folder by the front desk, but I don't know when someone last reviewed them. there's a first aid kit in the kitchen and a sign-in sheet for volunteers, not for visitors. please don't state that the open afternoon is approved, or assume we can put anything outside. say who could ask the landlord and what should be confirmed before we advertise a date. the likely date is the 14th, but we haven't said which month in the poster draft.

could you make this a practical plan with a week-by-week sequence for eight weeks, but keep the end date conditional on the landlord's answer. Include a short numbered section for the things that need a decision or confirmation, and separate immediate tasks from things that depend on expert advice. We have about £120 available, but that may need to cover printing and refreshments as well as supplies; don't assign the whole amount to clock materials. Give tasks an owner only where I've named someone or where you can phrase it as a volunteer role, and make clear that these are suggestions rather than agreed commitments. Don't calculate a value for any clock or add new staff, equipment, historical facts, repairs, or assurances. End with a brief list of open questions we should resolve at our next Tuesday meeting, including anything you can't infer from this request.", "output": "Create a practical, realistic eight-week plan for the volunteer-run antique clock room in the old Mercer Street print shop. The group has six volunteers, but usually only Jo, Malik, and the requester attend on Tuesdays. The room opens to visitors two Saturdays a month. A larger open afternoon is being considered for the 14th, but the landlord has not confirmed use of the back room, and the poster draft does not specify the month. Keep the event date and plan conditional where necessary. Distinguish actions that can begin now from decisions or permissions that are still needed. Treat suggested tasks as suggestions, not agreed commitments, and assign named owners only to people identified below; otherwise use a volunteer role.

### 1. Eight-week sequence
Provide a week-by-week sequence that fits the group’s limited time, including the possibility of spending one Tuesday on a shared records list. Show how the plan would prepare the room and visitors’ route before the possible open afternoon. Separate immediate tasks from tasks that depend on the landlord, electrical checks, or expert advice. Do not assume the event is approved.

### 2. Clocks, records, and safe care
There are 18 clocks: five wall clocks, four mantel clocks, three longcase clocks, and six small travel or desk clocks. One longcase has cracked glass and a label reading “please don't wind”; do not recommend testing or winding it. The other stops after about twenty minutes; Malik has not inspected its interior. Jo’s aunt owned the wall clock with the blue painted face, and there is no paperwork for it. There is a receipt for the small brass carriage clock, but its date is smudged. Do not invent dates, makers, values, or other history.

Recommend a simple record that volunteers can update after a visit and that distinguishes direct observations from information reported by others. Include a way to record uncertain details and who entered them. Existing records are in a notebook, two phone photo folders, and a spreadsheet last updated in January. Some notebook entries, such as “runs well,” lack dates and initials; many photos do not show the clock’s back, label, or condition. The group may be able to spend one Tuesday making a shared list, but not a whole day. Do not recommend discarding old notes or changing the spreadsheet before checking what is already there.

Suggest safe interim observations and labels for clocks that should not be touched. Jo can dust exterior cases with a dry cloth; Malik is comfortable checking whether a clock is already running. Neither is trained to oil or adjust a movement. Priya has offered to contact a local horologist, but availability and cost are unknown. Identify questions to ask the horologist without assuming they will visit or do the work. Do not advise taking clocks apart merely to demonstrate activity.

### 3. Room setup and visitor experience
Plan for a safe visitor route and arrangement of clocks, tools, and visitor materials before the possible event. The aisle beside the tall case is about 70 centimetres wide; the side door opens into that aisle and is the visitors’ exit. A low radiator is under the front window, with a box of old pendulums on the floor beside it. The ceiling lights sometimes flicker, especially when the kettle is on, and the socket near the display bench is loose. Ask the group to have the electrical issue checked; do not suggest that volunteers repair wiring. Available items are a folding table, two lamps, three paper signs, and a small lockable cabinet. There are no display stands, and the budget is limited, so do not assume substantial purchases.

Allow for a short explanation of how a mechanical clock works, but do not assume anyone has agreed to give a talk. Jo might welcome visitors. Malik may be able to demonstrate winding a clock that has been cleared for it, but does not want this treated as a promise. Make room for visitor questions, including the question asked last month: “Is the ticking meant to sound uneven?” The visitor did not identify which clock they meant. Avoid claiming that all clocks work or are original. The room has a magnifying glass, several old trade catalogues, and a printed map showing where some clocks were collected; two pencil marks on the map are unidentified.

### 4. Permissions, budget, and confirmations
The shop is rented. The landlord permits the regular Saturday openings, but nobody has asked about extra chairs, a pavement banner, or using the back room. The requester can ask about the landlord contact, but do not state that the event or any of these arrangements is approved. Identify what must be confirmed before advertising a date, including the month. Fire instructions are in a folder by the front desk, but their last review date is unknown. There is a first aid kit in the kitchen and a volunteer sign-in sheet, but no visitor sign-in sheet; do not infer additional requirements or claim these arrangements have been reviewed.

The available budget is about £120 and may also need to cover printing and refreshments. Do not allocate all of it to clock materials. Keep suggested spending modest and identify costs that need checking rather than assuming prices.

End with a brief open-questions list for the next Tuesday meeting. Include unresolved details that cannot be inferred from this request, and use a short numbered section to identify decisions or confirmations needed.
